title: Sliding Window Maximum: monotonic deque maintaining decreasing order.
shortTitle: Sliding Window Maximum: Monotonic Deque Maintaining Decreasing Order
keyPoints: Maintain a deque of indices with values in strictly decreasing order from front to back
Pop from the back any index whose value is less than or equal to the entering value
Evict the front index if it has slid out of the window (index <= right - k)
The front of the deque is always the index of the current window maximum
Store indices not values, because front eviction depends on position in the array
O(n) total time because each index enters and leaves the deque at most once

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a deque of indices with decreasing values; the front is always the window maximum, and each index enters and leaves at most once.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sliding Window Maximum** – return the maximum of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides across an array.
- **Monotonic deque** – a double-ended queue of indices maintained so the values at those indices are strictly decreasing from front to back.
- **Back eviction** – before adding a new index, pop from the back every index whose value is less than or equal to the new value.
- **Front eviction** – remove the front index if it has slid out of the window.
- **Complexity** – O(n) total time and O(K) space because each index enters and leaves the deque at most once.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India tracks a rolling K-minute peak of transaction rates. Rajesh keeps a short queue of candidate peak times, always ordered so the biggest is at the front. When a new, larger rate arrives, it knocks out every smaller candidate behind it. When a candidate falls out of the time window, it is removed from the front.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Monotonic deque on [10, 5, 12, 8, 15, 3, 7], k=3

  i=0: deque=[0]         values=[10]
  i=1: deque=[0,1]       values=[10,5]
  i=2: pop 1,0; push 2   deque=[2]       values=[12]
       result[0] = 12
  i=3: push 3            deque=[2,3]     values=[12,8]
       result[1] = 12
  i=4: pop 3,2; push 4   deque=[4]       values=[15]
       result[2] = 15
  i=5: push 5            deque=[4,5]     values=[15,3]
       result[3] = 15
  i=6: pop 5; push 6     deque=[4,6]     values=[15,7]
       evict front? 4 <= 6-3=3? No
       result[4] = 15

  Result: [12, 12, 15, 15, 15]

  Deque invariant (decreasing values):
  front ─── biggest ──── newest ─── back
  ┌───┬───┬───┐
  │15 │ 7 │   │  values always decrease
  └───┴───┴───┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sliding Window Maximum returns the maximum of every window of size K using a monotonic deque of indices kept in decreasing order of their values. For each new element, you pop from the back every index whose value is less than or equal to the new value, because those can never be the maximum while the newer, larger value is in the window. Then you push the new index, evict the front if it has slid out, and read the front as the window maximum.

Storing indices rather than values is essential because evicting the front depends on position. You need to compare the front index with the current window boundary to know when an element has aged out. The decreasing invariant guarantees the front is always the maximum: any smaller earlier value was already popped when a larger value arrived.

The headline property is O(n) total time. Each of the n indices is pushed once and popped at most once, giving at most 2n deque operations across the entire array. The deque never holds more than K indices, bounding space to O(K).

In the operations dashboard at the National Bank of India, Rajesh tracks the rolling peak transaction rate over every K-minute window to spot load spikes. The rate series streams continuously and is long, so recomputing each window's maximum from scratch would be too slow. The monotonic deque gives each window's maximum in amortized constant time per element, so the alert fires the instant the rate falls a set distance below the rolling peak.

Remember one sentence: maintain a decreasing deque of indices, pop smaller values from the back, evict expired indices from the front, and the front is always the window maximum.
